newsitem.title: HONG KONG: FEATURE-Hong Kong to open spectacular bridge for new airport.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Hong Kong to open spectacular bridge for new airport.

text.p: Britain's Margaret Thatcher will raise a toast and fireworks will be flying on Sunday as Hong Kong revels in the opening of a bridge to its US$20 billion new airport.
The Tsing Ma Bridge, or Lantau Link, will connect Hong Kong's largest island of Lantau, site of the new Chek Lap Kok international airport, with the rest of the territory.

The 1,377-metre long bridge, the second longest suspension bridge in the world after Britain's Humber bridge, will carry an eight-lane highway and a railway to transport people to the new airport once it opens and to the Tung Chung new town springing up around it.
The christening of a Hong Kong bridge may seem a small honour for a woman who negotiated the British colony's return to the mainland with the late Chinese leader Deng Xiaoping more than a decade ago.
But the new airport and associated infrastructure projects are a potent symbol of British and Chinese conflict and cooperation in the years leading up to the 1997 handover.
Hong Kong reverts to China at midnight on June 30 after more than 150 years of British colonial rule.
BUILDING CONCENSUS
Developing the airport and the roads and railways needed to get to it, plus the reclamation of hundreds of hectares of land from Hong Kong's harbour, has been a mammoth undertaking.
But the problems of building the airport -- one of the world's biggest infrastructure projects -- have been nothing compared with the political wrangling before the project's approval.
On June 30, 1995, two years to the day before Britain was to hand Hong Kong over to China, British and Chinese negotiators signed detailed agreements on the financing of the new airport.

The decision put an end to more than five years of often acrimonious debate, with saw Beijing accusing London of frittering away Hong Kong's funds on the project and Governor Chris Patten calling the talks "ridiculously tortuous negotiations."
A REALLY BIG SHOW

The Lantau Link fireworks display will attract thousands, possibly tens of thousands of people -- so many in fact that organisers have urged the less robust to stay home and watch the spectacle on television rather than risk being trampled on.
The former British Prime Minister will inaugurate the bridge as planned even though a section was damaged by saboteurs last week, raising fears about security and guerrilla attacks.
Mark Tam, information officer at the New Airport Projects Coordination Office, said the paen to the Lantau Link will be the last airport-related revelry under British rule.

"It is very likely that we will have to wait until the opening of the airport next year for another celebration," he said. The airport is expected to open in April 1998. By that time China will be the sovereign power in Hong Kong.
The Hong Kong Monetary Authority plans to issue a HK$10 coin to commemerate the bridge's inauguration, while the Post Office will offer a HK$5 stamp to mark the occasion.
OUT WITH THE OLD, IN WITH THE NEW
The gleaming new airport will be able to accomodate 35 million passengers per year from the day it opens. Eventually, it could be expanded to take on 87 million passengers per year.
It will also have the capacity to move three million tonnes of freight per year from the start and ultimately will be able to handle nine million tonnes.
Hong Kong's existing Kai Tak airport was designed to handle 24 million passengers per year but now squeezes in some 30 million. It processes 1.6 million tonnes of freight annually.
Because of capacity problems, Kai Tak rejects some 300 flight applications per week, making it harder for tourists and business people to come to Hong Kong and spend their money.
The airport, which is located on a sliver of reclaimed land jutting out from Hong Kong's populous Kowloon district, also shuts down late at night to allow local residents to get some sleep.
That means that airlines arriving late sometimes treat their passengers to a free night in a hotel -- in some other country.
Getting to the old airport also can be a headache. But by next June the railway will be speeding travellers to a new airport in air-conditioned comfort.
NOT EVERYONE IS HAPPY
All these features will cost airlines more. The Airport Authority aims to raise landing charges to almost twice what it costs the average aircraft to touch down in Kai Tak.
Airlines have angrily condemned the increases.

"The additional landing charges make the economics look terrible and the airlines may be forced to make a commercial decision and suspend marginal services," said Stanley Hui, chief executive officer at Hong Kong's Dragonair.
